text: You can now carry a peta-flop in your backpack.
In 2008, it filled a room and cost over a hundred million dollars.
So what changed? Rewind to 2008.
IBM's Roadrunner became the first computer to break a peta-flop.
Nearly 300 racks, 2.35 megawatts of power.
Now, Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra claims up to one peta-flop.
So, did a supercomputer just shrink into a backpack?
Here's the catch. Roadrunner counted in big, precise 64-bit numbers. NVIDIA's RTX Spark
chip hits its petaflop with tiny 4-bit numbers, plus a shortcut called sparsity. Same word,
very different math. So why care? Memory. Most laptops give the graphics chip its own
small memory. This one shares a single pool, up to 128 GB. Not all of it goes to graphics.
In one test, the GPU could reach about 110.
Enough to fit an AI model with 120 billion parameters on your lap, no cloud, no server room.
The bill, from $2,599.
The 128 gig version, 5,899.
So no, it's not a 2008 supercomputer.
It's an AI lab in a backpack.
Roadrunner drew 2.35 megawatts.
This one charges from a 140 watt brick.
This is Tech Minister.
